meta.subject: science
meta.description: Physics facts: Newton's laws, motion, energy, waves, circuits, thermodynamics, gravity, magnetism, optics, fluid mechanics, nuclear physics

facts.statement: Newton's First Law (Law of Inertia): An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion at constant velocity, unless acted upon by an unbalanced force
Newton's Second Law: Force equals mass times acceleration (F = ma)
Newton's Third Law: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction
Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist changes in its state of motion; objects with more mass have more inertia
The unit of force in the SI system is the Newton (N), which equals 1 kg x m/s^2
Net force is the sum of all forces acting on an object; if net force is zero, the object is in equilibrium
Friction is a force that opposes motion between surfaces in contact; it converts kinetic energy to thermal energy
Weight = mass x gravitational acceleration. On Earth, g = 9.8 m/s^2, so a 10 kg object weighs about 98 N
Mass measures the amount of matter in an object (kg); weight measures the gravitational force on it (N)
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity: a = (v_final - v_initial) / time
Velocity includes both speed and direction; speed is the magnitude of velocity
Momentum = mass x velocity (p = mv). It is conserved in collisions
Gravity pulls all objects toward the center of Earth (or any massive body) with force F = G(m1)(m2)/r^2
In free fall (ignoring air resistance), all objects accelerate at the same rate: 9.8 m/s^2 on Earth
Static friction prevents an object from starting to move; kinetic friction acts on an object that is already moving. Static friction is generally greater than kinetic friction
The impulse-momentum theorem states that the change in momentum of an object equals the impulse applied: F x t = m x delta_v
A push or a pull on an object is called a force; forces can cause objects to start moving, stop moving, or change direction
Gravity is a force that pulls objects toward the ground; it is why things fall when you drop them
Centripetal force is the inward force needed to keep an object moving in a circular path; it is directed toward the center of the circle
Angular momentum is conserved in a closed system; this is why an ice skater spins faster when pulling in their arms

common_errors.wrong: heavier objects fall faster than lighter objects
common_errors.correct: In the absence of air resistance, all objects fall at the same rate regardless of mass (about 9.8 m/s^2 on Earth).

common_errors.wrong: if something is not moving, no forces are acting on it
common_errors.correct: An object at rest can have multiple forces acting on it that are balanced (net force = 0).

common_errors.wrong: the action and reaction forces in Newton's Third Law cancel out
common_errors.correct: Action and reaction forces act on DIFFERENT objects, so they do not cancel out.

common_errors.wrong: mass and weight are the same thing
common_errors.correct: Mass is the amount of matter (kg), which stays the same everywhere. Weight is gravitational force (N), which changes with location.

common_errors.wrong: an object moving at constant velocity must have a force pushing it
common_errors.correct: An object at constant velocity has zero net force. Once moving, it continues without a push (Newton's First Law). Forces like friction slow it.

common_errors.wrong: heavier objects have more gravity
common_errors.correct: All objects with mass have gravity. More massive objects have stronger gravitational pull, but the acceleration due to gravity is the same for all falling objects.

common_errors.wrong: centrifugal force is a real outward force
common_errors.correct: Centrifugal force is a fictitious force felt in a rotating reference frame. The real force is centripetal force, directed inward toward the center of the circle.

common_errors.wrong: friction always slows things down
common_errors.correct: Friction can also cause motion. For example, friction between your shoes and the ground is what allows you to walk forward.

facts.statement: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion, calculated as KE = (1/2)mv^2
Potential energy is stored energy due to position or condition; gravitational PE = mgh (mass x gravity x height)
The law of conservation of energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed from one form to another
Work is done when a force moves an object: W = F x d (force times distance in the direction of the force)
Power is the rate at which work is done: P = W/t (work divided by time), measured in watts (W)
Chemical energy is stored in the bonds of molecules and released during chemical reactions like combustion
Thermal energy is the total kinetic energy of particles in a substance and is related to temperature
Simple machines (lever, pulley, wheel and axle, inclined plane, wedge, screw) make work easier by changing force direction or magnitude
Mechanical advantage = output force / input force. A lever with MA of 3 multiplies your force by 3
Elastic potential energy is stored in stretched or compressed objects like springs: PE = (1/2)kx^2
Nuclear energy comes from splitting atoms (fission) or combining them (fusion); the Sun produces energy by fusion
Efficiency = (useful energy output / total energy input) x 100%. No machine is 100% efficient due to friction
Heat transfers in three ways: conduction (direct contact), convection (fluid movement), and radiation (electromagnetic waves)
A roller coaster at the top of a hill has maximum potential energy and minimum kinetic energy; at the bottom, it has maximum kinetic energy and minimum potential energy
One joule is the energy required to move an object with a force of 1 Newton through a distance of 1 meter
Gravitational potential energy depends on height: the higher an object is above the ground, the more potential energy it has
Energy can change forms: a falling ball converts potential energy to kinetic energy; a lamp converts electrical energy to light and heat

common_errors.wrong: energy can be created from nothing
common_errors.correct: Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can only be converted from one form to another.

common_errors.wrong: heat and temperature are the same thing
common_errors.correct: Temperature measures average kinetic energy of particles. Heat is the transfer of thermal energy between objects at different temperatures.

common_errors.wrong: if you hold a heavy box still, you are doing work on it
common_errors.correct: Scientifically, work requires movement in the direction of the force. Holding a box still involves no displacement, so no work is done on the box.

common_errors.wrong: simple machines reduce the amount of work done
common_errors.correct: Simple machines make work easier but do NOT reduce the total work. They change the force or direction needed.

common_errors.wrong: cold is a form of energy
common_errors.correct: Cold is the absence of thermal energy, not a form of energy itself. Heat flows from warmer to cooler objects.

common_errors.wrong: a ball rolling on the ground will keep going forever
common_errors.correct: Friction and air resistance gradually convert kinetic energy to heat, causing the ball to slow down and stop.

common_errors.wrong: nuclear energy and atomic bombs are the same thing
common_errors.correct: Nuclear energy can be harnessed in controlled fission reactions in power plants to generate electricity. Atomic bombs are uncontrolled chain reactions.

facts.statement: A wave transfers energy without transferring matter
Wavelength is the distance between two consecutive crests or troughs; frequency is the number of complete waves per second (measured in Hertz, Hz)
Wave speed = frequency x wavelength (v = f x lambda)
Transverse waves vibrate perpendicular to the direction of travel (like light); longitudinal waves vibrate parallel (like sound)
Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids, and slowest in gases because particles are closer together in solids
The speed of light in a vacuum is approximately 300,000 km/s (3 x 10^8 m/s)
The electromagnetic spectrum includes (from longest to shortest wavelength): radio, microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma ray
Amplitude determines the energy of a wave: higher amplitude = more energy. For sound, higher amplitude = louder
Reflection occurs when a wave bounces off a surface; the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
Refraction is the bending of a wave as it passes from one medium to another due to a change in speed
The Doppler effect: a wave source moving toward you has higher frequency (pitch); moving away has lower frequency
Visible light spectrum (ROYGBIV): red has the longest wavelength, violet has the shortest
White light contains all colors of the visible spectrum; a prism separates white light into its component colors
Diffraction is the bending of waves around obstacles or through openings; it is more pronounced when the opening is similar in size to the wavelength
The speed of sound in air at room temperature is approximately 343 m/s (about 767 mph)
Ultraviolet (UV) light from the Sun can cause sunburn and skin damage; the ozone layer blocks most UV radiation
Sound waves are produced by vibrating objects; the human ear can hear frequencies between about 20 Hz and 20,000 Hz
Interference occurs when two waves meet: constructive interference increases amplitude, destructive interference decreases it

common_errors.wrong: sound can travel through space (a vacuum)
common_errors.correct: Sound requires a medium (solid, liquid, or gas) to travel. It cannot travel through the vacuum of space.

common_errors.wrong: louder sounds travel faster
common_errors.correct: The speed of sound depends on the medium, not the volume. Loudness (amplitude) does not affect speed.

common_errors.wrong: light always travels at the same speed
common_errors.correct: Light travels at its maximum speed in a vacuum. It slows down when passing through media like water or glass.

common_errors.wrong: radio waves and sound waves are the same type of wave
common_errors.correct: Radio waves are electromagnetic waves that travel through vacuum. Sound waves are mechanical waves that need a medium.

common_errors.wrong: microwaves are only used for cooking
common_errors.correct: Microwaves are also used for cell phones, WiFi, radar, and satellite communications.

common_errors.wrong: X-rays and gamma rays are the same thing
common_errors.correct: X-rays and gamma rays are both high-energy electromagnetic radiation but differ in origin: X-rays come from electron transitions, gamma rays from nuclear processes.

common_errors.wrong: infrared light is dangerous
common_errors.correct: Infrared radiation is generally harmless at normal levels. It is the heat you feel from the Sun or a campfire. Only intense concentrations can cause burns.

facts.statement: Ohm's Law states that voltage = current x resistance (V = IR)
Electric current is the flow of electric charge, measured in amperes (A)
Voltage (potential difference) is the energy per unit charge that drives current, measured in volts (V)
Resistance opposes the flow of current, measured in ohms
In a series circuit, components are connected end-to-end and the same current flows through each; if one breaks, the circuit is open
In a parallel circuit, components are connected in separate branches; each branch has the same voltage
Conductors (metals) allow electric current to flow easily; insulators (rubber, plastic, glass) resist the flow of current
Electric power = voltage x current (P = VI), measured in watts
Static electricity results from the buildup of electric charge on a surface, often through friction
Like charges repel each other; opposite charges attract each other
A complete circuit requires a source of energy, a load, and a continuous conducting path
Total resistance in series: R_total = R1 + R2 + R3. In parallel: 1/R_total = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3
An electromagnet is created by wrapping wire around an iron core and running current through it
Every magnet has a north and south pole; you cannot isolate a single magnetic pole
A semiconductor (like silicon) has conductivity between a conductor and an insulator; semiconductors are the basis of modern electronics and computer chips
Lightning is a massive electrostatic discharge caused by charge buildup in clouds; a single bolt can carry over 1 billion volts
Electric energy is calculated as E = P x t (power times time), measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh) for household billing
A fuse or circuit breaker protects a circuit by breaking the connection if too much current flows, preventing fires

common_errors.wrong: current is used up as it flows through a circuit
common_errors.correct: Current is not consumed. The same amount of current flows through a series circuit. Energy is transferred, but charge is conserved.

common_errors.wrong: batteries store electricity
common_errors.correct: Batteries store chemical energy that is converted to electrical energy through chemical reactions.

common_errors.wrong: electrons flow from positive to negative
common_errors.correct: Electrons flow from the negative terminal to the positive terminal. Conventional current flows positive to negative by historical convention.

common_errors.wrong: cutting a magnet in half gives you a north piece and a south piece
common_errors.correct: Cutting a magnet in half gives you two complete magnets, each with its own north and south pole.

common_errors.wrong: rubber is a perfect insulator
common_errors.correct: No material is a perfect insulator. Rubber is a very good insulator but can conduct at extremely high voltages.

common_errors.wrong: voltage and current are the same thing
common_errors.correct: Voltage is the pressure that pushes charges through a circuit. Current is the rate of flow of charges. They are related by Ohm's Law (V = IR) but are different quantities.

common_errors.wrong: touching a battery's terminals will always shock you
common_errors.correct: Household batteries (1.5V or 9V) have too low a voltage to push enough current through skin to cause a shock. High-voltage sources are dangerous.

facts.statement: The zeroth law of thermodynamics: if two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other
The first law of thermodynamics is the conservation of energy: the total energy of an isolated system is constant
The second law of thermodynamics states that entropy (disorder) of an isolated system always increases over time; heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold, never the reverse
The third law of thermodynamics states that as temperature approaches absolute zero, the entropy of a perfect crystal approaches zero
Absolute zero is 0 Kelvin (-273.15 degrees Celsius), the lowest possible temperature where particle motion is minimal
Specific heat capacity is the amount of energy needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1 degree Celsius; water has a high specific heat (4,186 J/kg-C)
Conduction transfers heat through direct contact between particles; metals are good conductors of heat
Convection transfers heat through the movement of fluids (liquids and gases); warm fluid rises and cool fluid sinks, creating convection currents
Radiation transfers heat through electromagnetic waves and does not require a medium; this is how the Sun's energy reaches Earth
An insulator like a thermos reduces heat transfer by minimizing conduction, convection, and radiation
Water's high specific heat capacity helps moderate coastal climates, making temperatures less extreme near oceans
The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero; to convert Celsius to Kelvin, add 273.15
A heat engine converts thermal energy into mechanical work; no heat engine can be 100% efficient (Carnot's theorem)

common_errors.wrong: cold flows into warm objects
common_errors.correct: Cold does not flow. Heat always flows from warmer objects to cooler objects. The warm object loses thermal energy.

common_errors.wrong: metal objects are colder than wooden objects at room temperature
common_errors.correct: Both are at the same temperature. Metal feels colder because it conducts heat away from your hand faster than wood.

common_errors.wrong: space is cold because there is cold air in space
common_errors.correct: Space is nearly a vacuum with almost no particles. Objects in space lose heat through radiation, not conduction or convection.

common_errors.wrong: you can reach absolute zero
common_errors.correct: The third law of thermodynamics implies that absolute zero can be approached but never actually reached.

common_errors.wrong: adding heat to a substance always raises its temperature
common_errors.correct: During a phase change (melting or boiling), added heat goes into breaking molecular bonds rather than raising temperature.

facts.statement: A concave (converging) lens is thinner in the middle and spreads light rays apart; it is used to correct nearsightedness
A convex (converging) lens is thicker in the middle and brings light rays together to a focal point; it is used in magnifying glasses and cameras
A concave mirror curves inward and can focus light to a point; it is used in telescopes and satellite dishes
A convex mirror curves outward and produces smaller, wider-view images; it is used in car side mirrors and store security mirrors
Objects appear to have color because they absorb certain wavelengths of light and reflect others; a red apple reflects red light and absorbs other colors
Opaque objects block light, translucent objects let some light through (frosted glass), and transparent objects let most light through (clear glass)
Shadows form when an opaque object blocks light; the shadow is on the side opposite the light source
Light travels in straight lines called rays; this is why shadows have sharp edges when the light source is small
The law of reflection states that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, measured from the normal (perpendicular) to the surface
Total internal reflection occurs when light hits a boundary at a steep angle and reflects entirely back into the denser medium; this is how fiber optic cables work

common_errors.wrong: we see objects because our eyes send out light
common_errors.correct: We see objects because light reflects off them and enters our eyes. Our eyes detect light; they do not emit it.

common_errors.wrong: a magnifying glass makes things bigger
common_errors.correct: A magnifying glass does not change the size of the object. It bends light rays to create a larger virtual image that your eye perceives.

common_errors.wrong: black is a color of light
common_errors.correct: Black is the absence of visible light. An object appears black when it absorbs all wavelengths of visible light and reflects none.

common_errors.wrong: mirrors reverse left and right
common_errors.correct: Mirrors reverse front and back, not left and right. The image appears reversed because you are facing the opposite direction from your reflection.

facts.statement: Pressure equals force divided by area (P = F/A); a smaller area with the same force creates higher pressure, which is why needles are sharp
Atmospheric pressure at sea level is approximately 101,325 Pascals (1 atmosphere), which equals the weight of air above that point
Archimedes' principle: an object immersed in a fluid is buoyed up by a force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces
An object floats if its density is less than the density of the fluid; it sinks if its density is greater
Density = mass / volume. Water has a density of 1 g/cm^3 (1,000 kg/m^3)
Pascal's principle states that pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted equally in all directions; this is the basis of hydraulic systems
Bernoulli's principle states that as the speed of a fluid increases, its pressure decreases; this helps explain how airplane wings generate lift
Ice floats because water expands when it freezes, making ice less dense (0.92 g/cm^3) than liquid water (1.0 g/cm^3)
Air pressure decreases with altitude because there is less air above pushing down; this is why your ears pop on an airplane
A barometer measures atmospheric pressure; a manometer measures the pressure of enclosed gases

common_errors.wrong: heavy objects always sink in water
common_errors.correct: Whether an object floats depends on its density, not just its weight. A heavy steel ship floats because its overall density (including air inside) is less than water.

common_errors.wrong: suction pulls things in
common_errors.correct: There is no such thing as suction as a force. When you use a straw, you reduce air pressure inside it, and atmospheric pressure pushes the liquid up.

common_errors.wrong: airplanes fly because the engines push them up
common_errors.correct: Airplane engines provide forward thrust. Lift is generated by the wing shape, which creates lower pressure above the wing and higher pressure below (Bernoulli's principle plus angle of attack).

common_errors.wrong: water always boils at 100 degrees Celsius
common_errors.correct: Water boils at 100 degrees C only at standard atmospheric pressure (sea level). At higher altitudes with lower pressure, water boils at a lower temperature.

facts.statement: Nuclear fission splits a heavy nucleus (like uranium-235) into smaller nuclei, releasing a large amount of energy; this powers nuclear reactors
Nuclear fusion combines light nuclei (like hydrogen) into heavier ones (like helium), releasing even more energy than fission; this powers the Sun and stars
Radioactive decay is the spontaneous emission of particles or energy from an unstable nucleus; the three main types are alpha, beta, and gamma radiation

Alpha particles are helium nuclei (2 protons, 2 neutrons), stopped by paper; beta particles are electrons or positrons, stopped by aluminum; gamma rays are high-energy photons, reduced by lead or thick concrete
Half-life is the time required for half of the radioactive atoms in a sample to decay; Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years
E = mc^2 (Einstein's equation) shows that mass and energy are interchangeable; a small amount of mass converts to enormous energy in nuclear reactions
A chain reaction occurs when the products of one nuclear reaction trigger additional reactions; in a nuclear reactor, control rods absorb neutrons to regulate the chain reaction
Radioactive dating uses the known half-life of isotopes to determine the age of rocks, fossils, and artifacts
Nuclear power plants produce no direct carbon dioxide emissions during operation, but they create radioactive waste that must be safely stored for thousands of years

common_errors.wrong: all radiation is dangerous and man-made
common_errors.correct: Radiation exists naturally everywhere (cosmic rays, radon gas, bananas contain potassium-40). Low levels of natural background radiation are normal and not harmful.

common_errors.wrong: nuclear power plants can explode like nuclear bombs
common_errors.correct: Nuclear reactors cannot produce a nuclear explosion. The fuel is not enriched enough. Reactor accidents involve meltdowns and radiation leaks, not nuclear detonations.

common_errors.wrong: after one half-life, all the radioactive material is gone
common_errors.correct: After one half-life, half remains. After two half-lives, one quarter remains. Radioactive material never fully disappears; it decreases exponentially.

common_errors.wrong: fusion and fission are the same process
common_errors.correct: Fission splits heavy atoms apart; fusion joins light atoms together. Both release energy, but through opposite mechanisms.
